code.title: A heap inside an array: parent and children by index arithmetic
code.python:
h = [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5]            # a min-heap written level by level
n = len(h)
print("heap array:", h)
ok = True
for i in range(n):
    # Index arithmetic replaces pointers: parent (i-1)//2, children 2i+1 and 2i+2.
    p, l, r = (i - 1) // 2, 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
    ps = "-" if i == 0 else str(h[p])
    ls = str(h[l]) if l < n else "-"   # "-" means no such node
    rs = str(h[r]) if r < n else "-"
    print("i=" + str(i) + " value=" + str(h[i]) + " parent=" + ps + " left=" + ls + " right=" + rs)
    if i > 0 and h[p] > h[i]:          # heap order: parent <= child
        ok = False
print("min-heap order holds:", "yes" if ok else "no")
# Time: O(N) to check every node. Space: O(1) extra.

followUps:
With 1-based indexing the root sits at index 1 and the formulas get simpler: the parent of i is i/2, and its children are 2i and 2i+1. Slot 0 is left unused (or holds a sentinel).

Example: the node at index 5 has parent 5/2 = 2 and children 10 and 11. The same node in a 0-based array is index 4, with parent (4-1)/2 = 1 and children 9 and 10.

Nothing else changes: the heap rules, O(log N) insert and extract, and O(1) peek are identical. You pay one wasted slot, and the last parent becomes index n/2 instead of n/2-1, which is a classic off-by-one when you mix the two styles.

The tree must be complete for two reasons: it lets the tree live in an array with no gaps, and it keeps the height at about log2N, which is what makes insert and extract fast.

No gaps: the index formulas only work if every position before the last one is filled. A tree with holes would need empty array slots; a chain of 5 nodes that always goes right would need indices 0, 2, 6, 14, 30, so 31 slots for 5 values.

Short height: a complete tree with 7 nodes has height 2. The same 7 nodes in a chain have height 6, so sift-up and sift-down would cost O(N) instead of O(log N).

This is also why insert always adds at the end and extract always removes the last element: both keep the shape complete.

code.title: Min-heap insert (sift up) and extract-min (sift down)
code.python:
h = []

def insert(x):
    h.append(x)                              # 1. put it at the end (shape stays complete)
    i = len(h) - 1
    while i > 0 and h[i] < h[(i - 1) // 2]:  # 2. sift up while smaller than the parent
        p = (i - 1) // 2
        h[i], h[p] = h[p], h[i]
        i = p

def extract_min():
    smallest = h[0]
    last = h.pop()                           # 1. take the last element out
    if h:
        h[0] = last                          # 2. move it to the root
        i, n = 0, len(h)
        while True:                          # 3. sift down: swap with the SMALLER child
            m, l, r = i, 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
            if l < n and h[l] < h[m]:
                m = l
            if r < n and h[r] < h[m]:
                m = r
            if m == i:
                break
            h[i], h[m] = h[m], h[i]
            i = m
    return smallest

for x in [5, 3, 8, 1, 4]:
    insert(x)
    print("insert", x, "->", h)
for _ in range(2):
    m = extract_min()
    print("extract-min =", m, "->", h)
# Time: O(log N) per insert or extract. Space: O(N) for the array.

followUps:
Because the child you swap up becomes the parent of the other child, so it has to be the smaller of the two; the left child is not always the smaller one.

Example: parent 9 with children 4 (left) and 2 (right). If you always swap with the left child you get 4 on top with children 9 and 2, and 4 > 2 breaks the heap rule. Swapping with the smaller child gives 2 on top with children 4 and 9, which is valid.

The cost is one extra comparison per level (child against child, then the smaller child against the parent), so sift-down does at most 2 comparisons per level and stays O(log N) time, O(1) space.

Lower the value where it sits in the array and then sift it up, because a smaller value can only be wrong relative to its parent. The hard part is finding its index, so you keep a map from item to its current position (an "indexed heap") and update that map on every swap.

void decreaseKey(int id, int newKey) {
  int i = pos[id];             // where the item sits now
  key[i] = newKey;             // must be smaller than before
  siftUp(i);                   // every swap also updates pos[]
}

Example: heap [1, 5, 3, 9]; decrease 9 to 2. It swaps with 5 and stops under 1, giving [1, 2, 3, 5].

Time O(log N), plus O(N) extra space for the position map. Without the map, finding the item is O(N). Library heaps (Java, Python, C++) have no decrease-key, so there you push a new entry and skip the stale one later.

code.title: Build-heap: count swaps for bottom-up heapify vs inserting one by one
code.python:
def sift_down(a, i, n):
    """Sift a[i] down inside a[0..n); return how many swaps it took."""
    swaps = 0
    while True:
        m, l, r = i, 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
        if l < n and a[l] < a[m]:
            m = l
        if r < n and a[r] < a[m]:
            m = r
        if m == i:
            return swaps
        a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]
        i = m
        swaps += 1

def bottom_up(n):
    a = list(range(n, 0, -1))              # n, n-1, ..., 1: worst case for a min-heap
    swaps = 0
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):    # last parent back to the root
        swaps += sift_down(a, i, n)
    return swaps

def one_by_one(n):
    a = []
    swaps = 0
    for k in range(n):                     # insert at the end, then sift up
        a.append(n - k)
        i = k
        while i > 0 and a[i] < a[(i - 1) // 2]:
            p = (i - 1) // 2
            a[i], a[p] = a[p], a[i]
            i = p
            swaps += 1
    return swaps

print("input: n, n-1, ..., 1 (descending)")
for n in [15, 1023, 65535]:
    print("n=" + str(n) + " bottom-up swaps=" + str(bottom_up(n)) + " one-by-one swaps=" + str(one_by_one(n)))
# Bottom-up: O(N) time (swaps stay below N). One by one: O(N log N). Space: O(1) extra.

followUps:
Because sift-down on a node only works if both of its subtrees are already heaps, and going backwards from the last parent guarantees the children are finished before their parent.

Example with [9, 8, 7, 1]. Backwards: index 1 first (8 swaps with its child 1) gives [9, 1, 7, 8]; then index 0 (9 sinks past 1, then past 8) gives [1, 8, 7, 9], a valid min-heap. Forwards: index 0 first (9 swaps with 7) gives [7, 8, 9, 1]; then index 1 gives [7, 1, 9, 8], and the root 7 is larger than its child 1. The small value was stuck below a node that had already been processed.

We start at n/2-1 because every index from n/2 on is a leaf, and a leaf is already a heap of size 1. That skips half the array for free.

Standard libraries use bottom-up heapify whenever you hand them a whole collection at once instead of adding items one by one.

  • Java: new PriorityQueue<>(collection) calls an internal heapify().
  • Python: heapq.heapify(list) turns a list into a heap in place.
  • C++: std::make_heap, and the priority_queue constructor that takes a range or a container.
  • C#: the PriorityQueue constructor that takes a sequence of (element, priority) pairs.
  • Heapsort: its first phase is exactly this build step.

Practical consequence: with 1,000,000 values, building from the collection costs O(N), about a million steps, while a loop of add calls costs O(N log N), up to about 20 million in the worst case.

code.title: Kth largest with a min-heap that never grows past K
code.python:
import heapq

nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4]
k = 2
print("nums: " + str(nums) + ", k = " + str(k))

heap = []                                  # heapq is a min-heap
for x in nums:
    heapq.heappush(heap, x)
    # Keep only the k largest seen so far: throw away the smallest of k+1.
    if len(heap) > k:
        heapq.heappop(heap)
    print("after " + str(x) + ": smallest kept = " + str(heap[0]) + ", size = " + str(len(heap)))
# The smallest of the k largest values is the kth largest.
print("kth largest:", heap[0])
# Time: O(N log K). Space: O(K).

followUps:
Quickselect partitions the array around a pivot like quicksort, but then continues only into the side that contains the wanted index. The kth largest is the element at index t = n - k of the sorted order.

int select(int[] a, int lo, int hi, int t) {
  int p = a[hi], i = lo;                  // Lomuto: pivot = last element
  for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) if (a[j] < p) swap(a, i++, j);
  swap(a, i, hi);                         // pivot lands at its final index i
  return i == t ? a[i] : i < t ? select(a, i + 1, hi, t) : select(a, lo, i - 1, t);
}

Example: [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2, so t = 4. Pivot 4 lands at index 3; 3 < 4, so search the right part [5, 6]. Pivot 6 lands at index 5; go left; index 4 holds 5, the answer.

Average O(N) time, worst case O(N2) on sorted input, so swap a random element into a[hi] first. O(1) extra space if written as a loop; it reorders the input.

Each machine finds its own top K, sends only those K values to one coordinator, and the coordinator picks the Kth largest of what it received.

This is correct because every value in the global top K is also in the top K of the machine that holds it. Example: K = 10 and 100 machines with a billion values each. Each machine runs a size-10 min-heap in O(n log K) and sends 10 numbers, so the coordinator handles 1,000 values instead of 100 billion.

Cost: the machines work in parallel, network traffic is 100 × K values, and the coordinator needs O(100K log K) time.

If K is huge (for example the median), sending K values per machine is too much. Then use rounds: pick a pivot, ask every machine how many of its values are larger, and narrow the range, like a distributed quickselect or a histogram of counts.

code.title: Max-heap in each language, and why the comparator b - a is a bug
code.python:
import heapq

values = [5, 1, 8, 3]
print("values:", values)

# heapq is always a min-heap, so store the negated value to get a max-heap.
max_heap = []
for v in values:
    heapq.heappush(max_heap, -v)
order = ""
while max_heap:
    order += " " + str(-heapq.heappop(max_heap))     # pop, do not iterate
print("max-heap poll order:" + order)

# Pitfall (Java, C++, C#): the comparator b - a overflows for far-apart values.
a, b = -2000000000, 2000000000
diff = (b - a + 2**31) % 2**32 - 2**31               # what a 32-bit int would hold
print("a = " + str(a) + ", b = " + str(b))
print("b - a as a 32-bit int: " + str(diff) + " (negative, so the order is wrong)")
print("safe compare(b, a) sign:", (b > a) - (b < a))
# Time: O(N log N) to push and pop N values. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Compare by the first key, and only when the first keys are equal compare by the next one. Most languages let you chain this instead of writing it by hand.

  • Java: Comparator.comparingInt((Task t) -> t.priority).thenComparing(t -> t.name); add .reversed() or Comparator.reverseOrder() on the key that should be descending.
  • Python: push tuples such as (priority, name); negate a number to reverse it.
  • C++: compare with std::tie(a.p, a.name) > std::tie(b.p, b.name) inside the comparator.

Example: (2, "b"), (1, "z"), (2, "a") come out as (1, "z"), (2, "a"), (2, "b"): priority decides first, the name only breaks the tie between the two 2s.

Use Integer.compare for each key, never subtraction. The comparator must be consistent, otherwise the heap order is silently wrong.

In Java use PriorityBlockingQueue: it is a heap with a lock around it, so many threads can add and take safely. A plain PriorityQueue is not thread-safe and can be corrupted by two threads sifting at the same time.

Things to know:

  • take() blocks while the queue is empty, which is what worker threads want.
  • It is unbounded, so put() never blocks. If producers are faster than consumers, memory grows; add your own limit (for example a semaphore).
  • For tasks that must wait until a time, use DelayQueue or ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor.

Other languages: Python has queue.PriorityQueue; C++ has none, so wrap std::priority_queue with a mutex and a condition variable. Each operation is still O(log N), plus the cost of taking one lock.

code.title: Merge K sorted lists with a min-heap of the current heads
code.python:
import heapq

lists = [[1, 4, 5], [1, 3, 4], [2, 6]]
for i, lst in enumerate(lists):
    print("list " + str(i) + ": " + str(lst))

# Heap entry = (value, which list, position in that list); tuples compare left to right.
heap = []
for i, lst in enumerate(lists):
    if lst:
        heapq.heappush(heap, (lst[0], i, 0))       # one head per list

merged = []
while heap:
    value, li, pos = heapq.heappop(heap)           # smallest of the K current heads
    merged.append(value)
    pos += 1
    if pos < len(lists[li]):
        heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[li][pos], li, pos))   # push its successor
print("merged:", merged)
# Time: O(N log K) for N values in K lists. Space: O(K) for the heap.

followUps:
Use the same heap-of-heads merge, but keep only a small buffer of each file in memory instead of the whole file.

  1. Open all K files and read one block (say 1 MB) from each.
  2. Put the first record of each file in a min-heap.
  3. Pop the smallest, append it to an output buffer, and push the next record from the same file, reading another block when that file's buffer runs out.
  4. Flush the output buffer to disk when it is full.

Example: 100 files of 10 GB each need about 100 MB of buffers, not 1 TB. Memory is O(K × buffer), time is O(N log K) comparisons, and all disk access is sequential.

If K is too large for the buffers or the open-file limit (say 10,000 files), merge 100 at a time into 100 bigger files, then merge those: two passes over the data.

A loser tree is a tournament tree built for K-way merging: the leaves are the current head of each sorted run, every inner node remembers the loser of the match played there, and the overall winner (the smallest head) is kept at the top.

After you output the winner, the next record from the same run enters at that leaf and replays only the matches on its path to the root. At each level it is compared with the stored loser, so that is one comparison per level, about log2K in total. A binary heap's sift-down needs up to two per level (child against child, then against the parent).

Example: K = 8 gives 3 comparisons per output record with a loser tree, against up to 6 with a heap.

The big-O is the same, O(N log K) time and O(K) space, but the constant is smaller, which is why external sorts and database merge steps often use it.

code.title: Median of a stream with two heaps (max-heap low half, min-heap high half)
code.python:
import heapq

stream = [5, 15, 1, 3, 8]
print("stream:", stream)

low = []    # smaller half as a max-heap (values stored negated)
high = []   # larger half as a min-heap
for x in stream:
    heapq.heappush(low, -x)
    heapq.heappush(high, -heapq.heappop(low))      # pass low's largest across, so low <= high
    if len(high) > len(low):
        heapq.heappush(low, -heapq.heappop(high))  # low keeps the extra element
    # Odd count: the middle is low's top. Even count: average of the two tops.
    if len(low) > len(high):
        median = float(-low[0])
    else:
        median = (-low[0] + high[0]) / 2
    print("add " + str(x) + " -> median " + format(median, ".1f"))
# Time: O(log N) per add, O(1) per median. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Use lazy deletion: do not search the heap for the value that leaves the window; write it down in a "to delete" map and throw it away only when it reaches the top of a heap.

  1. Keep a map delayed[value] = count and track the logical size of each heap yourself.
  2. When a value leaves, add it to the map and reduce the logical size of the half it belongs to (compare it with the top of low).
  3. Rebalance the two halves using the logical sizes.
  4. After every step, while the top of a heap is in the map, pop it and lower its count.

Example: window [1, 3, -1] slides and 1 leaves. 1 is buried in low, so mark delayed[1] = 1; it is physically removed later, when it surfaces.

Time is O(log N) amortised per step. The alternative is two balanced trees (C++ multiset, Java TreeMap with counts), which delete directly in O(log K).

Stop storing those numbers and just count them: keep an array of 101 counters for the values 0 to 100, plus two small containers for the rare values below 0 and above 100.

To add a number, increase one counter: O(1). To get the median, walk the counters and add them up until you reach the middle position: at most 101 steps, which is O(1) no matter how many numbers arrived.

Example: 1,000 numbers, 4 below 0, 990 inside the range, 6 above 100. The median positions are 500 and 501. Skip the 4 small ones, then walk the counters until the running total reaches 500.

Only when the middle position falls inside one of the outside groups do you need actual values, so keep those two groups sorted (a heap or a tree each). With 99% of the data inside the range that almost never happens. Memory drops from O(N) to O(101 + outliers).

For an exact p99 you only need to keep the largest 1% of the values: put them in a min-heap, and the top of that heap is the p99.

Each new value is compared with the top; if it is larger, push it. Whenever the heap holds more than 1% of the count, pop. Example: 10 billion events means a heap of 100 million values, about 800 MB as 64-bit numbers. That fits on one large machine, and each event costs O(log N).

If that is too much memory, do two passes over stored data: first count values into buckets to find which bucket contains the wanted rank, then load only that bucket's values and select inside it. If values are small integers (latency in milliseconds), an array of counts is exact with O(range) memory.

In practice most systems accept a tiny error and use t-digest or HDR histograms instead.

code.title: Trie: insert, exact search and prefix search (the part a hash set cannot do)
code.python:
nxt = [[0] * 26]      # nxt[node][letter] = child node, 0 means "no child"; node 0 is the root
is_end = [False]

def insert(w):
    node = 0
    for ch in w:
        c = ord(ch) - ord("a")
        if nxt[node][c] == 0:            # create the missing child
            nxt.append([0] * 26)
            is_end.append(False)
            nxt[node][c] = len(nxt) - 1
        node = nxt[node][c]
    is_end[node] = True                  # a word ends here

def walk(s):
    """Follow s from the root; return the node reached, or -1 if the path breaks."""
    node = 0
    for ch in s:
        node = nxt[node][ord(ch) - ord("a")]
        if node == 0:
            return -1
    return node

def yn(b):
    return "yes" if b else "no"

words = ["apple", "app", "bat"]
for w in words:
    insert(w)
print("words: " + ", ".join(words))
n = walk("app")
print("search(app): " + yn(n != -1 and is_end[n]))
n = walk("ap")
print("search(ap): " + yn(n != -1 and is_end[n]))    # a prefix, not a word
print("startsWith(ap): " + yn(walk("ap") != -1))
print("startsWith(bo): " + yn(walk("bo") != -1))
print("nodes used: " + str(len(nxt)))
# Time: O(L) per operation for a word of length L. Space: O(total letters * 26).

followUps:
A lot: every node carries 26 child slots whether they are used or not, so a node costs roughly 100 to 200 bytes even though most slots are empty.

Rough numbers: in Java, 26 references × 4 bytes = 104 bytes, plus the array header and the node object, comes to about 140 bytes per node. In C++ with 8-byte pointers it is 26 × 8 = 208 bytes.

There is one node per distinct prefix. One million words of average length 8 with little sharing can create up to 8 million nodes, so about 1 GB, while the words themselves are only 8 MB of text.

Ways to shrink it: store children in a hash map or a small sorted list (only used slots cost memory), use one flat int array for all nodes instead of objects, or compress chains of single children with a radix tree.

A radix tree (also called a compressed trie or Patricia tree) is a trie where every chain of nodes with only one child is merged into a single edge that carries a whole string instead of one character.

Example with "romane", "romanus" and "romulus": the root has one edge "rom"; from there one edge "an" leads to a node with edges "e" and "us", and another edge "ulus" ends the third word. That is 5 nodes below the root, where a plain trie needs 12 (r-o-m-a-n-e, then u-s, then u-l-u-s).

Lookup is still O(L): you compare edge labels a chunk at a time. Insert is a little harder, because a new word may split an edge in two (adding "romp" to a tree that holds only "roman" splits that edge into "rom" + "an").

It is used where keys share long prefixes: IP routing tables, the Linux kernel, Redis, and URL routers in web frameworks.

code.title: Autocomplete: walk the trie to the prefix, collect completions, keep the most popular
code.python:
words = ["car", "card", "care", "cat", "dog"]
count = [5, 9, 7, 3, 8]                 # popularity of each query
nxt = [[0] * 26]
word_at = [0]                           # word index + 1 stored where a word ends, 0 = none

def insert(idx):
    node = 0
    for ch in words[idx]:
        c = ord(ch) - ord("a")
        if nxt[node][c] == 0:
            nxt.append([0] * 26)
            word_at.append(0)
            nxt[node][c] = len(nxt) - 1
        node = nxt[node][c]
    word_at[node] = idx + 1

def collect(node, found):
    """DFS below a node: every word found there starts with the prefix."""
    if word_at[node] != 0:
        found.append(word_at[node] - 1)
    for c in range(26):
        if nxt[node][c] != 0:
            collect(nxt[node][c], found)

for i in range(len(words)):
    insert(i)
print("queries:" + "".join(" " + words[i] + "=" + str(count[i]) for i in range(len(words))))
prefix, k, node = "ca", 2, 0
for ch in prefix:                       # O(P) walk; 0 would mean no match
    node = nxt[node][ord(ch) - ord("a")]
found = []
if node != 0:
    collect(node, found)
found.sort(key=lambda i: -count[i])     # most popular first
top = "".join(" " + words[i] + "(" + str(count[i]) + ")" for i in found[:k])
print("prefix: " + prefix + ", completions found: " + str(len(found)))
print("top " + str(k) + ":" + top)
# Time: O(P + S log S), S = words under the prefix (a size-k heap makes it S log k). Space: O(S).
# Real systems store the top-k list on every node so a query is just the O(P) walk.

followUps:
Search the trie for words that are within a small edit distance (usually 1 or 2 changes) of what the user typed, instead of requiring an exact prefix match.

The standard way: do a DFS over the trie and carry one row of the edit-distance table for each node. The row says how far the letters on the path so far are from the typed text. If every number in the row is above the limit, skip that whole subtree.

Example: the user types "carx" with limit 1. The walk reaches "card", "care" and "cart" (one letter replaced), and drops the "dog" branch after the first letter or two.

Cost is O(nodes visited × L), far less than checking every word. At larger scale people precompute an index of words with one letter deleted (SymSpell) or use n-gram indexes. Then rank by popularity and closeness together, and only correct prefixes of 3 or more letters, since very short ones match everything.

A common setup is to rebuild the full trie offline every hour to once a day from the query logs, and to keep a small live layer for queries that started trending in the last few minutes.

Deploying it safely:

  1. Build the new trie as an immutable file away from the serving machines.
  2. Validate it: size close to the previous one, and known prefixes such as "wea" still return sensible results.
  3. Ship it to the servers and load it next to the old one.
  4. Switch a single pointer to the new trie (an atomic swap). Requests in progress finish on the old one, which is then freed.
  5. Roll out to a few servers first and keep the old file for instant rollback.

Because the trie is never modified while serving, readers need no locks. The price is memory for two copies during the swap, and results that are as stale as the rebuild interval.

code.title: Maximum XOR of two numbers with a binary trie (greedy on the opposite bit)
code.python:
nums = [3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8]
print("nums:", nums)

child = [[0, 0]]                          # flat trie: child[node][bit], 0 = missing
for x in nums:                            # insert each number as 31 bits, high to low
    node = 0
    for b in range(30, -1, -1):
        bit = (x >> b) & 1
        if child[node][bit] == 0:
            child.append([0, 0])
            child[node][bit] = len(child) - 1
        node = child[node][bit]

best = 0
for x in nums:
    node, cur = 0, 0
    for b in range(30, -1, -1):
        bit = (x >> b) & 1
        if child[node][bit ^ 1] != 0:     # opposite bit exists: this XOR bit becomes 1
            cur |= 1 << b
            node = child[node][bit ^ 1]
        else:
            node = child[node][bit]       # forced to take the same bit
    best = max(best, cur)
print("max xor (trie):", best)

brute = max(a ^ b for a in nums for b in nums)   # O(N^2) check of every pair
print("max xor (all pairs):", brute)
# Trie: O(31 * N) time and O(31 * N) nodes. All pairs: O(N^2) time.

followUps:
Use all 32 bits (bit 31 down to bit 0) so the sign bit is part of the path, and treat that top bit differently: there you want the same bit, not the opposite one.

Why: in two's complement, bit 31 set means the number is negative. An XOR result with bit 31 equal to 1 is negative, so for the largest signed result you want bit 31 of the XOR to be 0, which means pairing with a number that has the same sign. For bits 30 to 0 the usual "prefer the opposite bit" rule still applies.

Example: [-1, 0, 5]. The pairs give -1 ^ 0 = -1, -1 ^ 5 = -6 and 0 ^ 5 = 5, so the answer is 5. Blindly preferring the opposite bit everywhere would pick -1 ^ 0 (all 32 bits set), which is -1 as a signed int.

If instead the XOR is to be read as an unsigned 32-bit value, plain greedy over 32 bits is already right. Time O(32 · N), space O(32 · N) nodes.

Yes. Build the answer one bit at a time from the top, and use a hash set of number prefixes to test whether the next bit can be 1.

for (int b = 30; b >= 0; b--) {
  Set<Integer> pre = new HashSet<>();
  for (int x : nums) pre.add(x >> b);        // keep only the top bits
  int want = (ans >> b) | 1;                 // answer so far with this bit set
  for (int p : pre) if (pre.contains(p ^ want)) { ans |= 1 << b; break; }
}

It relies on one fact: if p ^ q = want, then p ^ want = q. So "are there two prefixes whose XOR is want?" becomes a set lookup.

Example: [3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8]. At bit 4 the prefixes are {0, 1} and want = 1; 0 ^ 1 = 1 is in the set, so bit 4 is kept. Continuing gives 28 (5 ^ 25).

Time O(31 · N), space O(N). Same big-O as the trie, usually less memory, but hashing makes it slower in practice.

code.title: Dijkstra with a min-heap and lazy deletion (stale entries are skipped)
code.python:
import heapq

n = 5
edges = [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 1), (2, 1, 2), (1, 3, 1), (2, 3, 5), (3, 4, 3)]   # (from, to, weight)
print("edges (from>to:weight): 0>1:4 0>2:1 2>1:2 1>3:1 2>3:5 3>4:3")
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for u, v, w in edges:
    adj[u].append((v, w))

INF = float("inf")
dist = [INF] * n
dist[0] = 0
pq = [(0, 0)]            # heap of (distance, node): the closest unfinished node comes out first
stale = 0
while pq:
    d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
    if d > dist[u]:      # lazy deletion: an old, worse entry for u
        stale += 1
        continue
    for v, w in adj[u]:
        nd = d + w
        if nd < dist[v]:
            dist[v] = nd
            heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v))   # no decrease-key: just push a better entry
print("shortest distances from 0:", dist)
print("stale heap entries skipped:", stale)
# Time: O(E log E) = O(E log V). Space: O(V + E).

followUps:
The rule "once a node comes out of the heap, its distance is final" stops being true, so Dijkstra can return wrong answers.

Dijkstra assumes that going further never makes a path shorter. A negative edge breaks that. Example: A→B costs 2, A→C costs 5, C→B costs -4. B is taken out first with distance 2 and marked done. Later C is reached at 5, and C→B would give 5 - 4 = 1, but B is already final, so the answer stays at the wrong value 2.

The lazy version without a "done" set will re-push B and may still end with correct numbers, but it can revisit nodes a huge number of times, and with a negative cycle it never stops.

Use Bellman-Ford instead, O(V · E), which also detects negative cycles. For many sources, Johnson's algorithm re-weights the edges to be non-negative and then runs Dijkstra.

When the graph is dense, meaning the number of edges is close to V2.

The array version has no heap: in each of V rounds it scans all V distances to find the closest unfinished node, then relaxes that node's edges. That is O(V2) in total, whatever E is. The heap version costs O(E log V), which becomes O(V2 log V) when E is about V2.

Example: V = 5,000 with nearly every pair connected, about 25 million edges. The array version does about 25 million simple steps. The heap version does about 25 million × 12 = 300 million, with heap pushes and extra memory on top.

Rule of thumb: prefer the array when E is more than about V2 / log V, and for small graphs stored as an adjacency matrix. For sparse graphs such as road maps (E about 3V), the heap wins easily.

code.title: Stable priority queue: order by (priority, arrival sequence number)
code.python:
import heapq

names = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]
priority = [2, 1, 2, 1, 1]                 # smaller number = more urgent
print("submitted:" + "".join(" " + names[i] + "(p" + str(priority[i]) + ")" for i in range(len(names))))

# Entry = (priority, seq, name). The seq tie-breaker makes equal priorities come out first-in, first-out.
pq = []
seq = 0                                    # grows by one for every submitted task
for i in range(len(names)):
    heapq.heappush(pq, (priority[i], seq, names[i]))
    seq += 1

out = ""
while pq:
    out += " " + heapq.heappop(pq)[2]
print("run order:" + out)
# Time: O(log N) per submit and per run. Space: O(N).

followUps:
Let waiting time count towards the ordering, so that a task that has waited long enough beats a newer task of higher priority.

A simple way that needs no re-sorting of the heap: compute the key once, at submit time, as key = submitTime + priority × penalty, and take the smallest key first. All waiting tasks age at the same speed, so their relative order never changes after insertion and the heap stays valid.

Example with penalty = 10 seconds: a low-priority task (5) submitted at t = 0 gets key 50. A high-priority task (1) submitted at t = 45 gets key 55, so the old task runs first. Submitted at t = 30 instead, the high-priority task gets key 40 and goes ahead.

Result: a task of priority p is overtaken only by tasks that arrive within p × penalty seconds of it, so no one starves. Still O(log N) per operation; keep the sequence number as the last tie-breaker.

A delay queue is a min-heap ordered by the time each task becomes ready, and a worker that sleeps exactly until the earliest of those times.

  1. Insert: push (readyTime, task) into the heap. If the new task is now the earliest, wake the worker so it can shorten its sleep.
  2. Take: look at the top. If its readyTime ≤ now, pop it and run it. Otherwise wait on a condition variable with a timeout of readyTime - now.

Example: tasks due at 10:00:05 and 10:00:02 are added at 10:00:00. The worker sleeps 2 seconds, runs the second task, then sleeps 3 more seconds and runs the first.

Insert is O(log N), peek is O(1), and no CPU is used while waiting. Java's DelayQueue and ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor work this way. Systems with millions of timers often use a timer wheel instead, which makes insert and cancel O(1).

code.title: Tokenizer-style longest-match lookup with a trie of vocabulary pieces
code.python:
nxt = [[0] * 26]
is_end = [False]

def insert(w):
    node = 0
    for ch in w:
        c = ord(ch) - ord("a")
        if nxt[node][c] == 0:
            nxt.append([0] * 26)
            is_end.append(False)
            nxt[node][c] = len(nxt) - 1
        node = nxt[node][c]
    is_end[node] = True

vocab = ["un", "believ", "able", "a", "b", "e", "i", "l", "n", "u", "v"]
for w in vocab:
    insert(w)
text = "unbelievable"
print("vocab: " + ", ".join(vocab))
print("text: " + text)

tokens = []
pos = 0
while pos < len(text):
    node, best_end = 0, -1
    # Walk the trie as far as the text allows, remembering the last place a token ended.
    for j in range(pos, len(text)):
        node = nxt[node][ord(text[j]) - ord("a")]
        if node == 0:                  # no vocabulary piece continues this way
            break
        if is_end[node]:
            best_end = j + 1           # longest match so far
    if best_end == -1:
        best_end = pos + 1             # unknown character: emit it alone
    tokens.append(text[pos:best_end])
    pos = best_end
print("tokens: " + " | ".join(tokens))
# Time: O(N * M), N = text length, M = longest vocabulary piece. Space: O(total vocabulary letters).

followUps:
Build a trie of the token sequences of every valid product ID, and at each generation step allow only the tokens that are children of the trie node you are currently at.

  1. Tokenize every valid ID with the model's own tokenizer and insert the token sequences into a trie.
  2. Start at the root. Before sampling each token, set the score (logit) of every token that is not a child of the current node to minus infinity.
  3. Sample, move to that child, repeat. Allow the end token only at nodes where an ID ends.

Example: valid IDs "AB-12" and "AB-17". After the model has produced "AB-1", only "2" and "7" are possible; everything else has probability 0.

The mask costs O(children of the node) per step and the trie takes O(total tokens in all IDs) memory. The output is valid by construction, so no retry loop is needed. For small lists, an enum in a structured-output schema does the same job.

Because the search has two different jobs: deciding which node to explore next, and remembering the best answers found so far. Each job wants the opposite end of the ordering.

  • Candidates: a min-heap by distance to the query. Its top is the closest node not yet expanded, so that is explored next.
  • Results: a max-heap limited to ef entries. Its top is the worst of the current best, so replacing it costs O(log ef).

The two tops also give the stopping rule: stop when the closest candidate is farther than the worst kept result, because nothing behind it can improve the answer.

Example with ef = 3: results hold distances 0.2, 0.4, 0.9. A neighbour at 0.5 beats 0.9, so 0.9 is evicted and the worst becomes 0.5. If the next closest candidate is at 1.1, that is more than 0.5 and the search stops.
